name: Ser Darrow of Edgemoor
appearance: Thirty-two, tall and rangy, with short dark hair that won't lie flat, a few days of dark stubble and grey-green eyes in a lean, weathered face. His nose was broken once and set a little crooked, with a faint scar across the bridge; his smile comes out dry and lopsided, and his laugh carries the length of a hall. At Saint Ysolde's he wears a plain linen infirmary shirt, often with a grey wool blanket round his shoulders, and gets up the way he does everything now: the good leg first, then the bad one, then the slow transfer, as if crossing a frozen pond. This week he walks the length of the hall without the stick, and he does not limp.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Ser Darrow: a man in his thirties with short dark hair, stubble, a nose once broken and set a little crooked, and a dry half-smile, a grey wool blanket around his shoulders over a linen shirt, in a stone infirmary hall with a fire on one side and a snowy mountain window on the other.
last_seen_doing: On the low wall-walk at nightfall, having kept Wren's count of the hall's lamps and promised to tell her first, next time he means to be brave.
now: He has answered to his name. He crossed the court to the bars in front of the whole House, called the Confessor back by both his names, and gave his own and his rank: nobody went down the far side, and nobody is going down this one. Marrant looked at his face through the bars, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour. The valley's story is dead at the gate; the Prior asked him only whether his shoulder was hurt. At the wicket his shoulder could not shut it and the knee said one thing, quite clearly; Maelis means to read it tonight. Before the hall, he went along the wall-walk after Wren, kept her count of the lamps while she told him how stupid it was, and promised to tell her first next time. Confessor Ivo Marrant and four grey cloaks are camped on the lower terrace below the gate, and the sixth of them keeps the winch-house.
story_so_far: With the Grace of the field-stone warm in his chest and sixty knights behind him, Darrow led the Ninth Lance into the Wend at Harrow Ford, laughing, until halfway across the warmth went out of him, his horse went down, and his knee gave with nothing touching it as he planted and turned toward the boy who had gone under his horse. As he went under he saw Aldric Vane's horse on the west bank, already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early. A red-handed clanswoman hauled him onto the east bank by his collar and made him look: the Wend carrying knights downstream, the Second Lance sitting untouched on the far shore, and a line of grey armored figures standing very still under the trees. Nineteen of the Ninth came home, and the Crown's heralds were already on the bell-house steps naming them the Faithless and bidding them kneel anew at the Oathspire. Carried up the Thousand Steps to the House of Menders, he chose Maelis Vorne's old art over the Crown's fast way, a strand of his own sinew bound in with emberthread, nothing given and nothing anyone can take back, and heard that he may never kneel again. Seven weeks on, walking without the stick, he learns that six grey cloaks with a cart and a censer are riding the Holloway toward the foot of the Steps with a list of the Faithless, and that when Wren was asked who was first on it, she looked at him. He asked to be sent down the Steps before the grey cloaks came and was refused a fifteenth time; he told the Prior to let the valley hear that the Faithless had gone down the far side, and she held Old Mercy silent so the gate would look as if it kept nobody. From the gate wall he watched the grey cloaks come in at the winch-house three bells early, and in the hour before dusk he stood among the wounded in the court while Confessor Ivo Marrant read his name first. He read the Confessor's trap a breath before it sprang and sent Wren for the bell, but the bell rang late: two grey cloaks came through the wicket, and his shoulder could not shut it on a third. When the bell stopped them and the Prior spoke the law of names, the Confessor made his camp on the lower terrace and called for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel. Darrow crossed the court to the bars and gave him his name.

quote.text: I was never much good at it anyway.

known_facts.fact: He captains the Ninth Lance, sixty knights and sixty squires, and has the fastest feet in the Lowmarch, having never once cared whose father mattered.
He and Aldric Vane rode knee to knee from the time they were squires and were knighted the same morning in the same cold chapel, palms on the warming Oathstone.
Before the charge he read the clan line as fleeing something in the trees behind them, coming through the ford rather than at it, and Hollis Garrow answered that the writ said clear the ford.
known_facts.evidence: They're coming through us

known_facts.fact: Halfway across the Wend the Grace went out of him in a single heartbeat, frost bloomed on his mail in midsummer, and when he planted his left foot and turned toward Tobin Marsh the knee gave with no blade and nothing touching it.
As he went under he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early.
The red-handed woman dragged him by the collar of his gambeson to the east bank among the standing stones, turned his head to the river, and told him in rough Vaelish to look and remember it.
Nineteen of the Ninth came back from Harrow Ford; he made himself count them, and he knows the names of the other forty-one and does not say them.

The surgeons of the Lowmarch pressed the knee, watched it slide, and sent him north, and four lay brothers carried him up the Thousand Steps on a litter, feverish, while Wren Ashdown counted the steps aloud beside him and insisted there are eleven hundred and seventeen.

The last of the road to the foot of the Steps was in a salt-cart driven by a woman the lay brothers called Rae, whom he watched because the fever had taken away his choice of what to watch, and would have watched without it; she talked to her oxen and not to her passengers, looked at his leg once the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, and told him as they lifted him that they would count him up and he should not help.

Maelis Vorne found the cord in the middle of the knee snapped rather than broken, and when he said it had held for thirty-two years she answered that it had help for twelve of them, and would not explain.
Offered the Crown's way or the Binding, he chose the Binding, an art the Crown burned the knowers of three hundred years ago, and was told he may not kneel for a long time, perhaps not ever.
A list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's was read out at the inn in Coldmere; Hollis Garrow is second on it, and when Hollis asked who was first, Wren did not answer and looked at Darrow.

From the infirmary window he knew the cart standing at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps, shafts up and two oxen in the snow, as the one he had ridden the last of the Holloway in, and he had not forgotten the one thing its driver said to him.

At the infirmary window the Reckoning showed itself to him for the first time, a pale gold script hanging over his palms that he could read though nobody had learned it in three hundred years, and behind his own numbers stood fainter ones whose owner he did not need to be told.
known_facts.evidence: He could read it anyway, and it was reading him

known_facts.fact: While Hollis hid the writ, the Captain was shut in a cell down the hall with Mender Vorne and nothing came through the door; Hollis has thought for a fortnight that a man could fight sitting down, if somebody taught him to stop looking at the floor.

Behind the cell door, Maelis told him of two fires a man can carry: one poured in, which the hand that poured it can take back, and one built by his own work, which cannot be poured or taken; the script he saw counts only the built one.
He knew the name of the burned order before she said it, from the curse the lowlands make of it, and she forbade him to say it in the hall, to Wren, to the Prior, or to Hollis most of all.
known_facts.evidence: The Emberwardens.

known_facts.fact: He argued that Hollis, second on the list and lying on his back when it is read, was owed the knowing of the built fire before he was; Maelis answered that Hollis is owed a leg and will get a wooden one, and that when Hollis asks, Darrow will lie to him. He took it.
known_facts.evidence: Then you'll lie to him.

known_facts.fact: He asked Hollis and Benedek why the Confessors chase the Faithless up a mountain if the Grace left them for faithlessness, and why mercy needs a list with his name first; he kept what Maelis told him behind his teeth.
Asked what the Grace did, he told Maelis: it made the river a road and every ache go quiet, and when it went it was cold, frost on his mail in midsummer. Asked whether he broke his oath, he said no.

He told Maelis the Grace did not go but was taken, since sixty men do not lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident; she agreed that then somebody took it, and said that what it did at the ford, and whose doing, she does not know.
known_facts.evidence: Sixty men don't lose a thing in the same heartbeat by accident

known_facts.fact: At Mother Ione's council he saw Sister Pell's cup chatter on the hearth before it settled, and read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge; nobody else looked.
known_facts.evidence: He read it before he meant to, the way he read a line before a charge. Nobody else looked.

known_facts.fact: Asked by Rae Thorne on the stair whether he rode a grey at the ford, he said yes and asked why; she did not say. He has not said Thistle's name since the river.
known_facts.evidence: He had not said her name since

known_facts.fact: At the council he asked to be put on the cage with the next load down before the grey cloaks reached the foot of the Steps, so the list would have nothing to climb for. Maelis answered for the fifteenth time, to the fire: the thread is soft, eleven hundred steps down are eleven hundred chances to tear it, and the cage is for salt. Rae said that down is where they are.
known_facts.evidence: the cage is for salt

known_facts.fact: Back from the council he read Hollis's hands as he had read Sister Pell's cup, asked once about them, was put off, and played him at knucklebones for a story told true; he caught the stone on the back of his hand, and Hollis paid: two days without a drink, three by the dusk bell.
known_facts.evidence: The bone sat on Darrow's knuckles

known_facts.fact: His answer, when Hollis said he had not known who to tell: that he had told the one man on the mountain who could not buy him a drink.
known_facts.evidence: the one man on this mountain who can't buy you a drink

known_facts.fact: Asked by Benedek to say the oath with him at the hour bell, only the words, he said go on, then; he had first said them kneeling in a cold chapel with Aldric Vane's shoulder against his and had not said them since the river, and they were still in him whole, by heart, and no use to anyone.
known_facts.evidence: whole, by heart, and no use to anyone

known_facts.fact: His lips moved with Benedek's and no sound came out of him; the lad was watching his mouth, not listening for his voice, and when they finished nothing came up through Darrow's hand, there being no stone under it.
known_facts.evidence: Darrow's lips moved with his

known_facts.fact: At the dawn bell his lips moved with Benedek's oath again, with Benedek watching his mouth.
known_facts.evidence: waited there until it moved with his

known_facts.fact: Asked by the Prior whether he told the valley story for the House or for the river, he said the river had had enough of them.
known_facts.evidence: The river's had enough of us.

known_facts.fact: The Prior asked him, because he reads a line before it moves, to tell Wren when, once the grey cloaks are at the bars; he said he would.
known_facts.evidence: You read a line before it moves

known_facts.fact: The low wall-walk beside the gate can be reached from the court without a stair, which is the whole of Maelis's reason for allowing him on it.
known_facts.evidence: the whole of Maelis's reason for allowing it

known_facts.fact: Through Pell's glass he read the grey cloaks' line: five strung along the last of the Holloway, their cart in the middle, and at the head a man whose saddle-bow trailed the censer's smoke.
known_facts.evidence: at the head a man whose saddle-bow trailed the censer's smoke

known_facts.fact: He told Rae Thorne to go down while the grey cloaks were an hour out and be on the road to Coldmere by dark; when she had let the road shut, he said her name and told her that had been her road.
known_facts.evidence: That was your road.

known_facts.fact: He told Rae Thorne he had asked fifteen times to go down those steps and she could walk down them today; it came out harder than he meant it to.
known_facts.evidence: Fifteen times I've asked to go down those steps.

known_facts.fact: When the Prior told him the law had been down since dusk, he had slept like a stone, and did not say so.
known_facts.evidence: He had slept like a stone.

known_facts.fact: On the wall after the grey cloaks came in, he stood until the knee went from stiff to sullen and shifted off it twice, which he did not think anyone had seen; when Rae sat on the gate-ward's bench, he sat at the other end before he had decided to.
known_facts.evidence: He sat at the other end before he had decided to.

known_facts.fact: He asked Rae Thorne why she had asked whether he rode a grey; she said carters look at horses, which he took for true and standing in front of another thing.
known_facts.evidence: true and still be standing in front of another thing

known_facts.fact: The mare's name came as far as his teeth and stopped; he had not said it since the river, and did not say it on the wall.
known_facts.evidence: He had not said it since the river

known_facts.fact: At the gate he stood among the wounded who could walk, at the foot of the gatehouse stair with his back to its post, where a man could lean without seeming to; nobody in grey looked at him when his name was read first.
known_facts.evidence: Nobody in grey looked at him.

known_facts.fact: When his name was read his weight came off the post: a flinch that Wren felt through his sleeve and Hollis saw from the window, and nobody else.
known_facts.evidence: His weight came off the post.

known_facts.fact: The Prior had asked him at the dawn bell to tell Wren when to have Old Mercy rung, once the grey cloaks were at the bars: a bell rung for nobody tells the valley there's somebody, and a bell rung too late tells the Confessors the gate is theirs.
known_facts.evidence: A bell rung too late tells the Confessors the gate is theirs.

known_facts.fact: He watched the Confessor's hands and the four men behind him, and the script, which until then had only ever read him, came up over his palms unasked and read the man at the bars: a fire all of it poured, and under the pouring nothing of his own; there was no lie in him, and the wicket was already open in his mind. Darrow said, 'Wren. Now.'
known_facts.evidence: Until that moment it had only ever read him.

known_facts.fact: He took the three strides to the wicket and put his shoulder to it beside the gate-ward's to shut it on a third grey cloak; the man leaned, the wicket threw Darrow off it against the gate, and the knee, deep in where the thread was, said one thing, quite clearly. Lay brothers and Rae Thorne shut it.
known_facts.evidence: said one thing, quite clearly

known_facts.fact: Going back to his post among the wounded, he passed the two grey cloaks who had come through the wicket close enough to touch, and neither of them looked at him twice.
known_facts.evidence: Neither of them looked at him twice.

known_facts.fact: Marrant called for him by name and rank to the whole court, as a man says a name he is sure of: come down and kneel, and the rest of the paper goes back into his cloak; he would wait.
known_facts.evidence: as a man says a name he is sure of

known_facts.fact: He crossed the court to the gate with the whole House watching and nobody stopping him, put his hand on the bars, and called the Confessor back from the head of the Steps by both his names.
known_facts.evidence: Darrow put his hand on the bars.

known_facts.fact: He gave his own name and rank through the bars, Darrow of Edgemoor, Captain of the Ninth, and told the Confessor he had read to a full bed: nobody went down the far side, and nobody is going down this one.
known_facts.evidence: You've read to a full bed.

known_facts.fact: Marrant came back to the bars and looked at his face, the first time anyone in grey had, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.
known_facts.evidence: the first time anyone in grey had

known_facts.fact: The Prior, who had heard her House's story die at her own gate, did not reproach him; she asked whether the shoulder was hurt.
known_facts.evidence: She asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.

known_facts.fact: From the window Hollis told him he had moved when his name was read, that he had seen it and nobody else had, and that he had walked up and given it anyway; Darrow did not ask him how he was.
known_facts.evidence: I saw it. Nobody else did.

known_facts.fact: Maelis looked at the knee first and then at his face, and told him the knee lies to her every morning and he hadn't, just now, and to keep it that way; she sent him to the hall slowly and said she would read the knee tonight.
known_facts.evidence: You didn't, just now.

known_facts.fact: Instead of going straight to the hall he went along the wall-walk after Wren, kept her count of the hall's lamps, nine, while she told him how stupid giving his name was, and promised to tell her first the next time he means to be brave.
known_facts.evidence: I'll tell you first.

relationships.label: his Mender
relationships.note: She tied the Binding with a strand of his own sinew and emberthread, reads the Knots with two fingers and her eyes shut, has told him fifteen times he may not go down the Steps, and it is she who will make him be honest, later, about how much he loved the charge.

relationships.label: of the Sixth Lance, on the next cot
relationships.note: He waved the writ at Darrow on the west bank and told him his head was not as fast as his feet; lost his right leg above the knee at the ford, cursed Darrow among many others on the carts north, and snores on his right at Saint Ysolde's, second on the list where Wren, asked who was first, only looked at Darrow. At the gate Hollis saw him move at his name, told him nobody else had, and called him Captain when he gave his name at the bars.

relationships.label: the girl with the ledger who counted him up the Steps
relationships.note: She counted the steps aloud beside his litter and would not let him say she had missed one; it was she who brought word of the grey cloaks, and who looked at him when Hollis asked whose name was first. After he gave his name at the bars she made him count lamps while she told him how stupid it was, and wrote down his promise to tell her first next time.

relationships.label: knighted the same morning
relationships.note: Squires together, knighted the same morning; at the ford Aldric told him to ride wider and seemed about to say more, and Darrow saw his horse already turned on the west bank; Darrow believes it was Aldric's hand that wrote his name first on the Confessors' list.

relationships.label: the youngest of the Ninth
relationships.note: Nineteen, who sang badly and constantly; when Tobin went under his own horse in the current, Darrow came off his mare and turned toward him, and that turn is where the knee went.

relationships.label: the woman who pulled him out
relationships.note: She looked at him alone across the water before the charge and called something the river took; afterward she hauled him to the east bank, made him look at what the Wend was carrying, and was gone when he turned back; he did not see her again for a long time.

relationships.label: the carter who drove him the last of the road
relationships.note: She talked to her oxen and not to him, looked at his leg once like a cracked wheel, and said one thing to him all day; seven weeks after the Binding he knew her cart at the winch-house from the window, and Wren says it was she who heard the list read and climbed through the night to bring it up.
